approved: Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Submarine Cable Protection) Bill 2013

Supported the Submarine Cable Protection Bill developed under Labor, noted Australia's 14 main international fibre pairs each carry between 1,000 and 2,000 gigabits per second, moved an amendment criticising the government's view that 25 megabit broadband speeds will be sufficient for households in future, and said half a million Australians remain in limbo over whether they will get fibre to the premises or to the node.

Supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Submarine Cable Protection) Bill 2013, noting Australia's seven submarine cables and three protection zones carry penalties of up to $66,000 and 10 years' imprisonment for individuals, and cited a 2008 Egypt cable-cutting incident that disrupted over 90 per cent of internet traffic between Europe and the Middle East.

Supported the shadow minister's amendment to the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Submarine Cable Protection) Bill 2013, citing an APEC report naming Australia a best-practice case study for submarine cable protection alongside Hong Kong and China, and cautioned against underestimating future technology needs.

Argued Labor's fibre-to-the-premises NBN model, with an expected 60-year fibre lifetime, is superior to the coalition's fibre-to-the-node plan, citing a BIS Shrapnel estimate that copper network maintenance costs up to $1 billion a year and could be cut by up to 70 per cent, and noted one in five Australians will be over 65 within the next 20 years.

Supported the bill regulating submarine cable protection, tracing the history of submarine cables from the first telegraph cable across the English Channel in 1851 to Australia's first connection via Java to Port Darwin in 1872, and described the 2000s cable investment boom and bust, in which Cable and Wireless shares fell from five pounds to 34 pence.

Supported the submarine cable protection bill, noting around 70 per cent of cable faults are caused by fishing and anchoring in waters less than 200 metres deep, and criticised the coalition's NBN plan for capping speeds at 25 megabits per second compared with Labor's 100, warning residents could pay up to $5,000 to connect fibre and citing a petition with 270,640 signatures calling for fibre to every home.

Argued the government's fibre-to-the-node NBN plan would deny Australians like a young constituent named Gretta, who has cerebral palsy, the independence that fibre-to-the-home technology could provide, and criticised the previous Liberal government for failing to upgrade communications infrastructure in 13 years, noting fibre-optic cable was first adopted for submarine cables in the 1980s.

Defended support for a national broadband network while criticising Labor's NBN Co. model as a costly failure, recounting the Brisbane City Council's privately funded fibre business model that the Rudd government ignored, and said Labor instead chose to spend more than $64 billion on a project that was never going to work.

Supported the Submarine Cable Protection Bill but criticised the government's fibre-to-the-node NBN alternative, cited ABS data showing fixed line data downloads grew about 63 per cent in the year to December 2012 and forecasts of a 4,300 per cent global data increase, and accused the Communications Minister of dropping Woodcroft in his own electorate from the revised NBN rollout map despite past promises.

Introduced summing-up of the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Submarine Cable Protection) Bill 2013, marking the 50th anniversary of the COMPAC undersea cable's opening on 3 December 1963 and its landing at Bondi Beach in the electorate of Wentworth, noting the project, later joined by the 1967 SEACOM cable, cost 33 and a half million pounds.
